articles.title: This Australian cave hid 25,000 years of ritual secrets
articles.summary: Microscopic plant remains are revealing how GunaiKurnai ancestors used Cloggs Cave for ritual practices over thousands of years. People deliberately gathered whole grasses, carried them into the dark cave, and burned them in thin layers, leaving behind traces that may span 25,000 years. A standing stone erected around 2,000 years ago and other ritual objects strengthen the evidence that the cave was a long-lived spiritual site.
articles.content:
The GunaiKurnai, an Australian Aboriginal nation, are recognized as the traditional custodians of Gippsland and the southern Victorian Alps. Caves within their lands have long been linked to spiritual practices. Accounts recorded in the 19th century, together with oral traditions, describe them as places where powerful learned women and men known as 'mulla-mullung', along with other spiritual practitioners, carried out rituals involving magic, healing, and cursing.

Archaeological evidence now shows that one of these sites, Cloggs Cave, was used for such activities over an extraordinary span of roughly 25,000 years.

"Here we show that the Old Ancestors selected whole grasses from the wider landscape and carried them into Cloggs Cave to spread out in thin layers and burn. Over time, sediments covered these burnt layers, preserving each layer on top of another over thousands of years," said Dr Elle Grono, a postdoctoral researcher at the Australian National University and the corresponding author of a new study published in Frontiers in Environmental Archaeology.

Microscopic Clues From Ancient Plants

Grono and researchers from Australia, France, and New Zealand examined phytoliths recovered from buried sediments inside Cloggs Cave. Phytoliths are microscopic silica structures that form within plant tissues and can survive long after the plants themselves have disappeared.

The research grew out of archaeological excavations carried out in 2019 and 2020. Those excavations were designed to determine how people collected and used plants inside the cave in the distant past. The work was requested by the GunaiKurnai Land and Waters Corporation, and GunaiKurnai representatives were involved in the research design, fieldwork, interpretation, and communication of the findings.

"Unlike pollen, which is dispersed by wind or insects, phytoliths mostly accumulate at the spot where a plant decays. No plants grow inside the cave due to a lack of light, so the phytoliths must have been carried in by people or by animals such as possums on their fur or through their scats," explained Grono. "We focused on half-burnt phytoliths from ashy layers, which can only have been brought in by people, as unburnt ones might have arrived through either means."

Because vegetation cannot grow naturally inside the dark cave, the burned plant remains offered especially strong evidence that people had intentionally carried grasses into the site.

Layers of Ash and a Standing Stone

Using microscopy, the researchers classified thousands of phytoliths collected from two excavation pits measuring 1.5 m and 2.3 m deep.

The upper sections of those pits contained 73 thin layers of ash deposited by people between approximately 4,400 and 1,600 years ago. Researchers established those ages using optically stimulated luminescence and carbon dating via accelerator mass spectrometry.

Hidden among the layers was another striking discovery: a standing stone measuring 28 cm high. Later analysis showed that Old Ancestors had intentionally placed the stone inside the cave for ritual purposes around 2,000 years ago.

Grasses Were Carefully Chosen

The team identified 29 different kinds of phytoliths representing grasses, herbs, and woody plants. Many were exceptionally well preserved, including delicate silica structures such as hair cells.

Grass phytoliths dominated the samples, accounting for as much as 97% of the total. They included members of the Pooideae subfamily, which favor temperate or cool conditions, as well as Panicoideae grasses, which generally thrive in warmer and more humid environments.

Phytoliths from Chloridoideae grasses, which tolerate drought and are adapted to warm, dry arid conditions, appeared less frequently. Remains from herbs and woody plants were also uncommon.

The pattern suggests that Old Ancestors did not simply gather whatever vegetation was nearby. Instead, they deliberately selected particular grasses.

Before European settlement, the landscape around Cloggs Cave included riparian forest and open woodland containing many different plant species. Yet those plants were largely absent from the archaeological deposits. The people using the cave instead chose grasses growing relatively close to its entrance.

"The phytoliths found at Cloggs Cave were from different parts of grass plants such as stems, leaves, flowers and roots, indicating that whole grasses were brought in, including the inedible parts," said Grono.

Evidence of Ritual Burning Across Millennia

As much as 18% of the phytoliths showed signs of burning or melting. Those altered plant remains occurred throughout the dated deposits, suggesting that people repeatedly carried vegetation into the cave and burned it there across the span of the past 25,000 years.

The finding fits with other archaeological evidence indicating that Cloggs Cave was a place of long-lasting ritual activity rather than an ordinary living site.

Professor Bruno David from Monash University, who co-led the excavations with GunaiKurnai Land and Waters Corporation, concludes that "their burning is consistent with GunaiKurnai traditional practices of using ash to perform magic and rituals, and also to track the footsteps of anyone coming in, including spirit-Beings. Other macro-botanical evidence, such as fat-smeared, trimmed wooden sticks from Casuarina trees, was also found in deeper and older deposits, indicating that other kinds of rituals using woody plants were also performed."
articles.reasoning: The article reveals significant archaeological evidence of the GunaiKurnai people's 25,000-year-old ritual practices, highlighting the preservation and recognition of Indigenous cultural heritage. This discovery has broad cultural and societal importance, fostering respect and awareness of Aboriginal traditions and history, with meaningful involvement of the GunaiKurnai community in the research process.

articles.title: Global inequality panel is a chance for research to change lives
articles.summary: Nature, Published online: 15 September 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-02885-8The scientific panel is welcomed. It must now invite all interested researchers to participate.
articles.content:
Luxury cars are an indulgence often out of reach for all but very wealthy people.Credit: Mike Kemp/In PIctures/Getty

Between 2000 and 2024, the richest 1% of people captured 41% of all new wealth. By contrast, just 1% was captured by the poorest 50%. These and other data on both income and wealth inequality were outlined in a commentary article published in Nature last week (J. E. Stiglitz et al. Nature 657, 345–348; 2026)

Why we need an International Panel on Inequality

Although income inequality has been falling, rising wealth inequality is a problem because it slows social mobility, feeds political polarization and erodes trust in institutions, say the article’s authors, who include Joseph Stiglitz, a Nobel-prizewinning economist at Columbia University in New York, and Winnie Byanyima, the head of the United Nations’ agency to combat AIDS, in Geneva, Switzerland.

It’s concerning that so much is known about the causes and damaging consequences of severe inequality but that this knowledge has failed to prompt meaningful action from politicians. The authors’ solution is for researchers to step up and be heard: they propose a body called the International Panel on Inequality (IPI). This would involve a group of around 40 specialists reviewing the research on inequality and putting the knowledge before policymakers.

The proposal for the panel has the backing of the UN and the African Union — along with more than 700 economists and other scholars of inequality. The governments of South Africa, Brazil, Spain and Norway are providing support.

The authors are calling for more governments to join them, and Nature urges them to do so, including by providing financial backing. We also encourage the IPI’s founding team to establish a transparent application process for participating on the panel. The founders’ ambition is for a diversity of voices to be represented. They must now establish an open process to fulfil this promise.

Tried and tested

The IPI team plans to examine government policies that are designed to lower inequality, including those that have worked and those that haven’t, and understand and report on the reasons behind the outcomes. Data on income and wealth are typically collected using household surveys. But two groups in society tend to have low response rates to surveys — the wealthiest and the poorest.

These groups are, arguably, among the most important to inequality research. Various researchers are testing collection methods other than surveys, such as administrative data from records of taxes and welfare benefits. Such data might yield more accurate information, but the work is scattered. A review of the evidence by one body would be a valuable endeavour.

How to end poverty and protect Earth: inside the debate tearing up economics

The inequality panel is inspired, in part, by the UN-affiliated Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC) in Geneva. It reviews global research on the causes and extent of climate change, on climate impacts and on the costs of climate action, periodically reporting back to its member governments. It’s a tried and tested method for providing robust scientific evidence to policymakers, but there are significant, and important, differences between how the IPCC functions and how the inequality panel would operate.

The team proposes that the IPI would also be a UN-affiliated body, but it would be attached to the United Nations University — a global think tank in Japan that does research to benefit member states. Unlike the IPCC, the authors do not suggest that the IPI will be an intergovernmental panel. This means that governments will not sign off on summaries of its reports, which happens with the IPCC. For the IPI, the panel members would assume this role.

There are benefits to greater independence from governments, especially at present. The IPCC was established in 1988, when the cold war meant that there were still marked geopolitical tensions, but when countries disagreed much less on scientific issues than they do today — both Russia and the United States appointed researchers to participate in the IPCC. That has now changed, with the US exit from the IPCC during Donald Trump’s second presidency, amounting to a huge loss of US research capacity from the panel’s work. As a more-independent body, IPI’s leadership would be free to choose its authors and reviewers from any country and reach conclusions on the basis of the evidence reviewed.

Why there needs to be a global debate on inequality

But there’s one aspect in which the IPI should follow the IPCC model: it needs to be open to researchers who want to participate, in the way that a climate scientist can apply to participate as an IPCC reviewer. The organization regularly puts out calls for expertise. Being an IPCC author or editor requires a nomination by government and is more complicated, but the rules and methods are publicly available.

The study of inequality, like all fields, includes debate and disagreement. There are researchers who regard a degree of inequality as necessary for economic growth, and those who take almost the opposite view. There is tremendous value when researchers from different perspectives assess studies in a spirit of collegiality. It will help to ensure that conclusions represent the best consensus of specialists.

The proposed IPI is the best chance so far for inequality research to inform policy action that can change lives for the better. It must ensure open opportunities for those who wish to be considered as members. This is also important for credibility. The diversity of voices that the IPI wishes to achieve will be key to good outcomes and, importantly, will help to build confidence among a wide group of stakeholders in those outcomes.
articles.reasoning: The article discusses the establishment of an International Panel on Inequality (IPI) aimed at consolidating global research on wealth and income inequality to inform policymakers. The panel's design to be independent, inclusive, and transparent promises a meaningful impact on policy and social justice, representing a substantial and hopeful step toward reducing inequality.

articles.title: The Mercator map has distorted Africa’s size for 450 years. The UN just voted to replace it.
articles.summary:
BY THE OPTIMIST DAILY EDITORIAL TEAM On most world maps hanging in classrooms, conference rooms, and government offices around the world, Greenland and Africa look roughly the same size. The reality is that they are not. Greenland covers about 2.2 million square kilometers while Africa covers 30.4 million. The map has been wrong by a […]
The post The Mercator map has distorted Africa’s size for 450 years. The UN just voted to replace it. first appeared on The Optimist Daily: Making Solutions the News.
articles.content:
BY THE OPTIMIST DAILY EDITORIAL TEAM

On most world maps hanging in classrooms, conference rooms, and government offices around the world, Greenland and Africa look roughly the same size. The reality is that they are not. Greenland covers about 2.2 million square kilometers while Africa covers 30.4 million. The map has been wrong by a factor of 14 since 1569, and on September 5, 2026, 164 countries voted to replace it.

The resolution, called “Correct the Map,” was sponsored by Togo with backing from the African Union’s 54 member states and passed in the UN General Assembly with support from France, the United Kingdom, and most of the world. One country voted against it (the United States). Another six nations abstained.

Why the Mercator map distorts

The Mercator map was designed in 1569 by Flemish cartographer Gerardus Mercator to help European explorers navigate across the globe. Its distortion is a mathematical consequence: it is impossible to represent the surface of a sphere accurately on a flat page without making compromises somewhere. The Mercator projection accommodates Earth’s curvature by making countries near the equator appear smaller than they are, and countries near the poles appear larger.

The result is a map where Greenland looks as large as Africa, Russia appears to stretch endlessly across the top of the world, and Europe sits comfortably at the center. None of those impressions are accurate.

The campaign group #CorrectTheMap has put the scale of the error plainly: you could fit the United States, China, India, Japan, Mexico, and much of Europe inside Africa and still have land to spare.

The Equal Earth projection

In 2018, a team of cartographers developed the Equal Earth projection as an alternative. The projection maintains the relative sizes of all landmasses with far greater accuracy, showing Africa in something close to its true proportions. In February 2026, the African Union’s 54 member states formally adopted it, describing it as a more accurate representation of all continents, particularly Africa.

The UN resolution is non-binding, meaning no country is legally required to change its maps. But the expectation is that institutions around the world, from international bodies to national education systems, will begin using the Equal Earth projection in place of the Mercator.

French Foreign Minister Jean-Noël Barrot announced that France’s ministry would stop using the Mercator map. Togolese Foreign Minister Robert Dussey, one of the resolution’s architects, described the stakes in a single sentence: “A fair world begins with a fair map.”

Barrot’s framing was more philosophical. “Changing the map obviously doesn’t change the world,” he said. “But correcting a representation that distorts it is already an act of truth.”

The US objection

US representative Yaryna Ferencevych said the resolution mocked the work and purpose of the General Assembly. “Instead of focusing on genuine problems of international peace, prosperity, or good relations, this body is debating map projects from the 16th Century, and their role in promoting reparations and ‘cognitive justice,'” she said.

The US was also the dissenting voice in March when the UN adopted a resolution declaring the transatlantic slave trade “the gravest crime against humanity.”

More than a cartographic error

For advocates of the change, the problem runs deeper than geographic inaccuracy. “Africa’s misrepresentation on world maps is not just a cartographic error. It is a narrative issue,” said Lerato Mogoatlhe of Africa No Filter, one of the groups behind the campaign. She described it as part of the world’s longest-running misinformation about the continent.

Kenyan geographer Kioko Muendo has made a similar argument: the Mercator map has implicitly downplayed Africa’s resources, population, and investment potential for generations. A continent that appears small on a map tends to be imagined as peripheral. The Equal Earth projection makes it difficult to sustain that impression.

The projection went from creation to UN resolution in eight years. Whether the institutions that educate students, brief diplomats, and frame international policy follow through quickly or slowly will determine how much practical difference the vote ultimately makes.

articles.personality_presentation:

This map makes places near the poles, like Greenland, look much bigger than they really are, while places near the equator, like Africa, appear smaller. Because of this, Africa has often been shown as about the same size as Greenland, even though Africa is 14 times larger in reality.

**What happened** – On September 5, 2026, the United Nations General Assembly voted to replace the Mercator map with a newer map called the Equal Earth projection. This vote was supported by 164 countries, including all 54 members of the African Union. Only the United States voted against it. The new map was created in 2018 and shows countries and continents in their true sizes much better than the old map.

For example, France has already decided to stop using the old map. Over time, schools, governments, and international groups may adopt the new map, helping people everywhere see a more accurate picture of the world.

**One-sentence takeaway** – The UN’s decision to replace the Mercator map with the Equal Earth projection marks a key step toward fairer and more accurate world maps that better represent Africa’s true size.

articles.personality_presentation_fr:

**Ce qui s’est passé** – Le 5 septembre 2026, l’Assemblée générale des Nations Unies a voté pour remplacer la carte de Mercator par une nouvelle carte appelée la projection Equal Earth. Ce vote a été soutenu par 164 pays, y compris les 54 membres de l’Union africaine. Seuls les États-Unis ont voté contre. La nouvelle carte, créée en 2018, montre les pays et continents à leur taille réelle beaucoup plus précisément que l’ancienne.

**Impact** – Ce changement est important car l’ancienne carte donnait une mauvaise idée de la taille et de l’importance de l’Afrique. En montrant l’Afrique plus petite qu’elle ne l’est vraiment, la carte de Mercator a contribué à des idées fausses sur la population, les ressources et le rôle du continent dans le monde. Utiliser la projection Equal Earth aide à corriger ces fausses impressions, ce qui peut influencer la manière dont les gens apprennent sur l’Afrique, comment les pays coopèrent et comment le continent est valorisé mondialement.

**Prochaine étape** – Bien que le vote de l’ONU ne soit pas contraignant, de nombreux pays et organisations devraient commencer à utiliser la carte Equal Earth à la place de la Mercator. Par exemple, la France a déjà décidé d’abandonner l’ancienne carte. Avec le temps, les écoles, gouvernements et groupes internationaux pourraient adopter la nouvelle carte, aidant ainsi les gens à voir une image plus juste du monde.

**Résumé en une phrase** – La décision de l’ONU de remplacer la carte de Mercator par la projection Equal Earth marque une étape clé vers des cartes du monde plus justes et précises qui représentent mieux la vraie taille de l’Afrique.
articles.personality_title_es: La ONU vota para reemplazar el mapa distorsionado por uno que muestra el tamaño real de África
articles.personality_presentation_es:
**Contexto** – Durante más de 450 años, el mapa de Mercator se ha usado ampliamente para mostrar el mundo. Este mapa hace que los lugares cerca de los polos, como Groenlandia, parezcan mucho más grandes de lo que realmente son, mientras que lugares cerca del ecuador, como África, se ven más pequeños. Por eso, África a menudo se muestra de tamaño similar a Groenlandia, aunque en realidad es 14 veces más grande.

**Qué pasó** – El 5 de septiembre de 2026, la Asamblea General de las Naciones Unidas votó para reemplazar el mapa de Mercator con un mapa más nuevo llamado proyección Equal Earth. Esta votación contó con el apoyo de 164 países, incluidos los 54 miembros de la Unión Africana. Solo Estados Unidos votó en contra. El nuevo mapa fue creado en 2018 y muestra los países y continentes en sus tamaños reales mucho mejor que el mapa antiguo.

**Impacto** – Este cambio es importante porque el mapa viejo daba una idea equivocada sobre el tamaño y la importancia de África. Al mostrar a África más pequeña de lo que realmente es, el mapa de Mercator contribuyó a malentendidos sobre la población, los recursos y el papel del continente en el mundo. Usar la proyección Equal Earth ayuda a corregir estas ideas falsas, lo que puede afectar cómo las personas aprenden sobre África, cómo trabajan los países juntos y cómo se valora al continente a nivel mundial.

**Próximo paso** – Aunque la votación de la ONU no es obligatoria, se espera que muchos países y organizaciones comiencen a usar el mapa Equal Earth en lugar del Mercator. Por ejemplo, Francia ya decidió dejar de usar el mapa antiguo. Con el tiempo, las escuelas, gobiernos y grupos internacionales podrían adoptar el nuevo mapa, ayudando a que las personas vean una imagen más precisa del mundo.

**Resumen en una frase** – La decisión de la ONU de reemplazar el mapa de Mercator por la proyección Equal Earth es un paso clave hacia mapas mundiales más justos y precisos que muestran mejor el tamaño real de África.
articles.image_prompt: A detailed warm-toned painting of two world maps side by side on aged parchment: the left map shows the distorted Mercator projection with an oversized Greenland and small Africa, while the right map shows the Equal Earth projection with Africa vastly larger and accurately proportioned, both maps glowing softly to symbolize truth and fairness.
